records.c: Use A to index the one-character file names at $0423, then load that PRG at its own load address from drive 8. $0440 is the one-byte SETNAM buffer.
One byte per PRG name, read by load_named_file. The table runs from A through Z, followed by 0, 1 and 2.
Set the title-entry flag, initialise the disk environment, load and display the bitmap, relocate file B, load the resident files, then load stage zero and call the engine.
Re-enable the KERNAL and select the loading display. Load the four files for the returned stage selector, update the operand at $8101 and re-enter the game.
Convert the loader's zero-based selector in $FF to the engine's one-based level and store it in the LDY immediate operand at $8101.
Select VIC bank $C000, screen $E800 and character set $D800, clear four screen ranges to spaces and set the initial prompt's colour.
Write PRESS FIRE from the stored legend to the loading screen with screen-code conversion. Wait on the active-low fire bit of CIA1 port A.
Convert the stored REWIND TAPE TO 000 legend to screen codes and copy it to $E99B.
Convert the stored PRESS PLAY ON TAPE legend and copy it to the loading screen at $E9EB.
Draw RESET TAPE COUNTER at $E94B and set each prompt cell's colour to white.
Four fixed-width loading messages beginning with PRESS FIRE. The disk bridge copies these to screen RAM after masking to six-bit screen codes.

records.d: S PLAY ON TAPEREWIND TAPE TO 000

records.c: Blank the display and dispatch $FF values 0 through 4 to four calls of load_named_file. The groups are J–M, N–Q, R–U, V–Y and Z, 0, 1, 2.
Bank out I/O and copy sixteen pages from $4000 to the RAM at $D000, patching the high bytes of both absolute indexed operands after each page.
Display the multicolour bitmap at $2000. Copy the colour matrix to $0C00 and the second colour plane to colour RAM from the tail of the bitmap load.
Select VIC bank zero, silence the SID, turn off sprites and CIA interrupt sources, restore the KERNAL RAM vectors, make ROM visible and blank the display.

File I contains 64-byte sprite records. Rendered frames include a sword user, running poses and animal shapes. This span covers pattern storage at $0F00–$0FFF.

Glyph overlay mask table ORed into the second strip at $4730 by $9CAA.
Glyph overlay mask table ORed into the first strip at $4700 by $9CB3.
World X high byte for 32 object slots. File D supplies these seeds before the stage initializer applies the loaded spawn data.
World X low byte for 32 object slots. File D supplies these seeds before the stage initializer applies the loaded spawn data.

Object event latch for 32 object slots. File D supplies these seeds before the stage initializer applies the loaded spawn data.
Seed for four projectile slots, with groups for activity, direction, timer and coordinate bytes. $AF30 finds a free entry and installs a new trajectory here.
The first twelve bytes hold the old character IDs while the sword overlay draws over them. The next eight bytes hold the CIA1 matrix readings.
Indexed initial colour values for the two generated playfield screen matrices. $83E7 and $83F0 use the tables pointed to by $E280 and $E300.
Authored initial bytes for the bottom of the first screen matrix. The engine regenerates this matrix from metatiles and writes sprite pointers at $4BF8.
The first two 64-byte slots in file E after the playfield matrix. This RAM is also the base used by the runtime sprite copier's patched operands.
Common VIC bank $4000 sprite image slots for the gameplay display. Rendered patterns include limbs, weapon strokes and small airborne shapes. This span covers pattern storage at $4C80–$4FFF.
Common VIC bank $4000 sprite image slots for the gameplay display. Rendered patterns include limbs, weapon strokes and small airborne shapes. This span covers pattern storage at $5000–$53FF.

File E's initial copy of the alternate playfield matrix. The redraw code updates it while the other matrix is visible. The bottom eight bytes are its runtime sprite pointers.
Jump to the music initialiser at $7D71. A selects the tune preset.
Pass the requested sound-effect number in A to $7FE0.
Jump to $7E52, which changes the audio mode and clears its enabled flag.
Three entry points jump to the routines at $70D8, $70DB and $70E1 to set, clear or read the audio setting at $70E5.
Read the mode bits at $70ED to choose the two active sound update paths. With neither bit set, clear all three SID gate registers.
Jump to the three-voice sound-effects updater at $7E5D.
Credit string embedded near the sound driver, naming Mark Tait for music and code.
records.d: MUSIC AND CODE (C) MARK TAIT. LT

records.c: Use the master divider and the per-voice duration counters to decide when to fetch the next music event. A nonnegative byte is a note. $FE stops the tune and $FF reinitialises its preset. Other negative bytes index the command handler table.
Two-byte music command target, the current voice slot and one trailing byte. The dispatcher patches the address then jumps through it.

Add the voice's transposition to the note, resolve its frequency and read the duration. Advance the sequence pointer, retrigger the gate when voice settings allow it and initialise the per-note modulation counters.
When fading is enabled, count down to the next SID volume change. Reload the delay and stop scheduling changes once the volume reaches zero.
Release the voice gate at the programmed duration threshold. For an enabled pitch envelope, index its waveform and pitch sequences and update the pending frequency.
For voice 1 when the sweep is enabled, adjust the SID cutoff high byte by $7183 each tick. Change direction when the arithmetic would carry or borrow past the end.
Use enabled per-voice counters to alternate control values and, in the special rhythmic phase, switch frequency and SID filter mode.
Apply the short pitch decay and temporary control-register changes for enabled voices. The attack effect raises pitch by seven table steps before restoring the base note.
Use the voice's phase counters and step sizes to add or subtract from its pending frequency and pulse-width words.

If enabled, step through the four arpeggio offsets and look up the resulting note. The slide check clamps when the target high byte equals the current high byte and its low byte is smaller, irrespective of direction. Otherwise add or subtract the step based on the direction flag.
Advance the enabled pulse-width counters, then write the prepared frequency and pulse widths for all three voices to the SID.
Double the note index in A, then fill voice X's frequency low and high buffers from the interleaved SID note table.
Set or clear the audio setting byte at $70E5 through overlapping entry points. The entry at $70E1 reads it back.
Seed values for the chosen audio mode, modulation offsets and volume fade state. The sound tick tests the activity flags at $70EB and $70ED.
SID register base offsets for voices 1, 2 and 3.
Current tune index and tick division followed by the per-preset modulation periods and duration modes.
Initial per-voice stream pointers, gate-release flags and thresholds, repeat counters and saved pointers for the transposed-pattern call and return.
Three-byte voice groups for pending frequency, pitch and pulse-width oscillator state, counters and modulation steps.
Voice control bytes followed by note counters and flags for sliding pitch, pitch decay and short waveform changes.
Initial pulse widths, cutoff sweep state and arpeggio offsets used by the per-tick sound update.
Voice state for gate-retrigger suppression, pulse widths, pitch slides, arpeggios, repeat counts and sequence pointers.
Working per-voice pattern, percussion and waveform counters. The last three bytes hold the individual voice filter-routing bits.
Seven eight-byte offsets into the pitch and control streams for the percussion-envelope command.
First eight-byte pitch offset case in the source; the paired first control sequence follows it.
Interleaved eight-byte pitch and SID control sequences. The tick selects a percussion voice envelope through $70E6,X and reads both values at the same phase.
Attack/decay and sustain/release preset bytes indexed by the percussion command at $76BC.
Interleaved frequency low and high bytes. The note helper doubles its input before indexing these words.
Three six-byte index tables for stream-pointer, voice-state and envelope presets, respectively.
Ten bytes per envelope preset. Six bytes go to the SID voices' attack/decay and sustain/release registers. Four set the divider and initial control bytes.
Five eighteen-byte tables copied into the sequencer's initial voice-state arrays by $7DDA.
Five six-byte tune entries, each with low bytes for the three voice stream addresses followed by the corresponding high bytes.
Increment the 16-bit music stream pointer at $F0/$F1 by one.
Advance the current music stream pointer by Y plus one, including the opcode.
Enable the master-volume fade and use the next byte as its divider, then advance to the next stream event.
Set the per-voice gate-release flag and read its duration threshold from the next byte of the event.
Clear the per-voice duration-triggered gate-release flag.
Enable the short pitch-decay effect and set both envelope registers to $0A.
Clear the per-voice pitch-decay flag.
Select SID control byte $42 for the current voice.
Select SID control byte $50 for the current voice.
Select SID control byte $40 for the current voice.
Select SID control byte $10 for the current voice.
Set the current voice's stored control byte to zero.
Select rising pitch, then read the step, divider and target note. Convert the transposed target note to a SID frequency word.
Select falling pitch, then share the rising-slide command's operand parser.
Set the arpeggio flag and read its two note offsets from the music stream.
Clear the current voice's arpeggio flag.
Clear both direction flags used by the pitch slide.
Read the pulse-ramp step and secondary mode, enable the ramp and turn off the pulse-width oscillator.
Clear the pulse-ramp flag and its secondary mode.
Read the pulse oscillator divider, step and cycle length. Set its midpoint to half the cycle length and disable the separate pulse ramp.
Clear the pulse-width oscillator flag.
Read register/value pairs until register marker $AF and write each value to the selected SID offset.
Read the repeat count and remember the current stream pointer just after this command.
Decrement the repeat count and jump back to the saved pointer until the count reaches zero.
Read the two bytes of the voice's initial pulse width.
Set the master track divider and the current preset's duration-scaling flag from the next two bytes.
Enable the alternation between the current note and a filtered noise phase.
Clear the flag that alternates the note and filtered noise phase.
Set the delayed waveform change flag for this voice.
Clear the delayed waveform change flag.
Read repeat count, transposition and target address. Save the following stream address and begin decoding the target pattern.
Repeat the called pattern until its loop count expires, then restore the caller's stream pointer and clear transposition.
Set the initial cutoff high byte, initialise sweep direction and read its step value.
Clear the cutoff sweep flag and toggle the current voice's SID filter routing bit.
Enable the short waveform substitution driven by $7172.
Clear the waveform substitution driven by $7172.
Set up pitch modulation from a divider and frequency step and enable its per-voice flag.
Clear the current voice's pitch modulation flag.
Set the flag that suppresses retriggering the SID gate on a note.
Clear the gate-retrigger suppression flag.
Use the command's low three bits to choose a pitch envelope offset and ADSR pair. Enable the pitch envelope and reset its phase.
Clear the pitch envelope and restore pulse waveform with attack/decay $09 and sustain/release $07.
Enable the brief pitch increase at the start of the current voice's note.
Disable the brief start-of-note pitch increase.
Interleaved addresses of the interpreter's control-event handlers. The sequencer masks off the high bit of the command before doubling it to reach a vector.
Music event sequence from $7787 through $78DB. Note values are followed by duration bytes. High-bit values select interpreter commands, and the final $FF reinitialises the tune preset.
Music event sequence from $78DC through $7A55. Note values are followed by duration bytes. High-bit values select interpreter commands, and the final $FF reinitialises the tune preset.
Music event sequence from $7A56 through $7AA6. Note values are followed by duration bytes. High-bit values select interpreter commands, and the final $FF reinitialises the tune preset.
Music event sequence from $7AA7 through $7AD3. Note values are followed by duration bytes. High-bit values select interpreter commands, and the final $FE ends the tune.
Music event sequence from $7AD4 through $7AEB. Note values are followed by duration bytes. High-bit values select interpreter commands, and the final $FE ends the tune.
Music event sequence from $7AEC through $7B45. Note values are followed by duration bytes. High-bit values select interpreter commands, and the final $FE ends the tune.
Music event sequence from $7B46 through $7BA3. Note values are followed by duration bytes. High-bit values select interpreter commands, and the final $FE ends the tune.
Music event sequence from $7BA4 through $7BAB. Note values are followed by duration bytes. High-bit values select interpreter commands, and the final $FE ends the tune.
Music event sequence from $7BAC through $7BB6. Note values are followed by duration bytes. High-bit values select interpreter commands, and the final $FE ends the tune.
Music event sequence from $7BB7 through $7C2B. Note values are followed by duration bytes. High-bit values select interpreter commands, and the final $FF reinitialises the tune preset.
Music event sequence from $7C2C through $7D02. Note values are followed by duration bytes. High-bit values select interpreter commands, and the final $FF reinitialises the tune preset.
Music event sequence from $7D03 through $7D70. Note values are followed by duration bytes. High-bit values select interpreter commands, and the final $FF reinitialises the tune preset.
Load the tune's three stream pointers and its voice presets, program attack and release envelopes and filter registers, then reset the voice counters and enable the music dispatch.
Set the sound dispatch to $20 and clear the audio setting at $70E5.
For each active effect voice, read the next note and control values through its two stream pointers. Write frequency and control to the SID or clear the slot at the $FF terminator.
Six groups of three bytes for active flags, event indices, and the low and high bytes of note and waveform stream pointers.
Sound effect 0 has 8 note indices and an $FF stop byte. The tick doubles each note index to read its frequency word.
One SID control byte per note for sound effect 0. The paired effect stream supplies the frequency at the same index.
Sound effect 1 has 17 note indices and an $FF stop byte. The tick doubles each note index to read its frequency word.
One SID control byte per note for sound effect 1. The paired effect stream supplies the frequency at the same index.
Sound effect 2 has 3 note indices and an $FF stop byte. The tick doubles each note index to read its frequency word.
One SID control byte per note for sound effect 2. The paired effect stream supplies the frequency at the same index.
Sound effect 3 has 7 note indices and an $FF stop byte. The tick doubles each note index to read its frequency word.
One SID control byte per note for sound effect 3. The paired effect stream supplies the frequency at the same index.
Sound effect 4 has 4 note indices and an $FF stop byte. The tick doubles each note index to read its frequency word.
One SID control byte per note for sound effect 4. The paired effect stream supplies the frequency at the same index.
Sound effect 5 has 30 note indices and an $FF stop byte. The tick doubles each note index to read its frequency word.
One SID control byte per note for sound effect 5. The paired effect stream supplies the frequency at the same index.
Sound effect 6 has 18 note indices and an $FF stop byte. The tick doubles each note index to read its frequency word.
One SID control byte per note for sound effect 6. The paired effect stream supplies the frequency at the same index.
Sound effect 7 has 8 note indices and an $FF stop byte. The tick doubles each note index to read its frequency word.
One SID control byte per note for sound effect 7. The paired effect stream supplies the frequency at the same index.
Sound effect 8 has 16 note indices and an $FF stop byte. The tick doubles each note index to read its frequency word.
One SID control byte per note for sound effect 8. The paired effect stream supplies the frequency at the same index.
Two nine-byte tables of attack/decay and sustain/release values indexed by the effect number.
Four bytes per effect. The first pair points to its note sequence and the second pair points to its SID control sequence.
If the audio setting allows effects, choose the first available voice among 0 and 1, otherwise voice 2. Install the note and control pointers and initialise the SID voice envelope from preset A.
File F ends with 167 zero bytes after the effect-start routine's return at $8057.
Y selects the stage. Clear zero page, blank the screen and sprites, run the title path when $0200 requests it, install game raster and NMI vectors and initialise the stage.

Update the intro and scroll state, then the player, other objects, collisions and display preparation. Scan the keyboard and wait for the raster handshake. On exit, branch to a restart on stage 1 or return to the disk bridge.
Set the title and loop-exit flags at $0200 and $C2, clear $02FF and restore registers before RTI.
Acknowledge the raster IRQ, schedule $8269 at line $AD, select the playfield bank and one of its two screen matrices, apply fine scrolling and call the audio updater.
Schedule the playfield handler at line $26, prepare VIC bank $C000 for the panel, wait for the vertical split near $B5 and publish the prepared sprite positions, colours and pointers.
Blank the display, initialise audio and objects, patch the stage colours, generate graphics lookup tables and prepare the opening sprite arrangement and screen.
Set $7E and wait for the panel handler to clear it after committing the new draw state.
When the opening flag is one, move the stage-one opening sprites upward and right. When the opening ends, clear the intro flags and start the selected gameplay audio.
For object X, translate its position plus the A and Y sample offsets to a metatile column and row. Read the map through the patched address at $8517 and return the cell's property byte from $F500.
For every byte, reverse its eight individual bits into $EA00 and reverse the order of its four two-bit pairs into $EB00.
Use the object descriptor indexed by A to set the player image number from its third byte and the counter at $1420 from the new image's fourth byte.
Clear prepared sprite fields, collect visible objects and expand the player descriptor. Replace its form pointers with the working phase-dependent sprite slots.
Copy expanded descriptors from the visible-object list to selected sprite slots. The event flag gates whether to draw the ordinary companion or an additional foreground object.
Combine each sprite's expansion, high X and multicolour bits into the four VIC register bytes.
When the opening animation is finished, copy the calculated drawing state into the arrays the raster handler writes to the VIC.
Copy all eight prepared pointers to both screen matrices. Publish colours, coordinates, expansion, X high bits and multicolour flags to the VIC and enable all eight sprites.
Count down the second object's current image. Look up the next image and its duration, and place it relative to the player with four direction offset tables.
Combine the player's phase and pose to index three separate sprite-pattern pointer tables. Send each result to the copier for the corresponding working sprite slot.
Patch the source and destination addresses of a 63-byte sprite copy. In the reflected path choose the mono or multicolour reversal table and use the permutation at $C81A to mirror the byte columns.
Toggle the low bit of $80, which other object routines read as a phase flag.
Copy the seven 32-byte tables at $F600–$F6DF into object-coordinate, image and state arrays. Initialise the additional per-object counters while stepping down through slots 31 to 1.
Keep the fire bit from the decoded joystick in $28, separate from the directional bits.
Scan eight CIA1 keyboard columns. Handle the pause key with a release wait. The separately gated stage-selector cases set $FF and discard one return address to leave the engine.
On stage 1, decrement $81 and reload it with 3 when it expires. Exchange the 32-byte glyph strips at $4520 and $4540 to animate the terrain.
Replace the byte in $52 with five times its old value plus $3D, modulo 256. Return the new value in A.
Probe two positions on the player's centre column. If the map-cell index returned in Y is $FF, clear health.
When health changes, clear the panel's twelve health cells, then fill its segments in pairs of glyphs from the current value.
Spend one life, reset the timer and start the transition music. Rearrange the prepared sprites, animate their positions with the raster handshake and wait for the stop-music mode.
Restore the gameplay sound and starting health, reset event and player-action state and reload the current area's positions. With zero lives, copy the score for the title and request the title.
Use area $4A to restore the player's two 16-bit world coordinates and the camera's two 16-bit origin coordinates from eight split tables.

On a sub-area change reset the timer and queue effect 6. Decrement the timer with decimal arithmetic and write timer, score and the remaining-lives digit to the panel. At zero spend one health unit and reload $0999.
Compare the eight saved keyboard readings with $CE51. If all match, latch $02FF. While latched, colour the border and restore health to 7.

Read port 2 through $DC00, invert the five active-low input bits and translate them through $C7C8. Store the full action code in $27 and the low directional nibble in $20 before applying movement-state gates.
On an existing action, dispatch it immediately. Otherwise align the player with the ground, sample two foot positions, and enter falling state 2 with no support or jumping state 1 on up input.
For horizontal direction 1 or 2, sample both feet for the slope tile properties 3 and 5. Convert the input to its diagonal code and seed the slope-motion state and offsets.
For movement codes 9, 4, 5, 6 and 10, test the appropriate terrain sample. Select the diagonal traversal, land or turn animation and its counters, or cancel blocked movement.
Sample two vertically separated points on each side for property 1 or 8. Depending on the side, choose action 9 or 14 and clear the slope offsets before dispatch.
For action 1, test headroom at the facing-dependent X offset. While rising, use the remaining counter to index the upward deltas, switching into state 10 on a terrain hit.
For action 2, test both feet and step through the falling deltas while the two points are clear. On contact, arm the landing animation and sound and set action 3.

Action 3 handles the landing countdown, ground probes and alignment with the terrain. Depending on the slope beneath the player, prime the corresponding horizontal and vertical state before normal movement.
Decrement the traversal counter for action 4, adjusting direction and animation until it expires. Use the terrain probe and vertical movement table to decide the next displacement.
Advance action 5's traversal phases, falling back to terrain-based state selection after its timer. The running path derives a Y displacement from the terrain probe.
Handle the timed action 6 transition and select its image. While active, sample upper and lower terrain to choose the directional movement.
Update the countdown and sample terrain for action 7. On expiry, return to the normal movement path.
For action 9, check movement away from the edge and inspect terrain at several heights. Adjust pose and direction, detach, or enter the action 15 traversal when its path is clear.
For action 10, align the low Y nibble. Test the head-contact terrain and either hold the pose, change to an adjacent state on up input, or begin falling on down input.
Decrement the action 11 counter and set the next action or its movement code before applying the common position update.
Advance the timed action 12 transition. On expiry or either blocking terrain result, select action 13 and set its phase and image timer to 8.
Use the countdown and collision probe to continue action 13 or clear it and return to the common direction update.
For action 14, mirror the side selection of action 9. Sample terrain along the other edge and choose whether to detach, remain on the edge or enter a traversal animation.
Use action 15's countdown and terrain test to finish its animation or adjust its vertical displacement.
Run the final timed traversal state. Restore normal terrain-state selection on expiry or use the sampled property to choose a vertical displacement.
Update the player's 16-bit position using four movement delta tables indexed by the action nibble. Update facing and the walking image, then advance the view movement logic.
When the player crosses a horizontal tracking threshold, make the camera origin follow the player's X with an offset. Clamp or reset origins beyond the horizontal limits.
Track the player's vertical distance from the view origin. Pick upward or downward camera movement, include the falling action's compensation, clamp Y and update the pose adjustment.
Keep the player within the immediate left and right world limits before dispatching the stage-specific camera rules.
Translate the player and camera together at two stage-one coordinate gates. Arm the corresponding area events and constrain the camera around a horizontal seam.
Test stage-two boundaries and rectangles and relocate the view and player through its linked regions. At the event rectangle, save object 15's coordinates and arm the area's event state.
Check two stage-three view rectangles. One gives the player and view fixed destination coordinates. The other adds a fixed offset to both coordinate pairs.
Test two view gates on stage four and translate both the player and camera by fixed offsets so the relative screen position is preserved.
Apply the stage-five view translation and arm its area events. The final area saves the original position of object 15 before advancing the event.
Enter the slope alignment routine when the player has a slope flag and no active traversal action.
Align the player to a 16-pixel Y grid then test the two foot positions for slope properties 3 and 5. Apply a slope correction indexed by the low X nibble and seed the appropriate slope motion.
When the sword overlay is inactive, latch its mask offset and wait for a new fire edge before requesting effect 5 and entering the draw path.
Wait for the raster flag and choose the current screen matrix. Translate the player's screen position to cells, save twelve original characters and install the sword overlay tile IDs.
Copy the twelve saved character patterns into the working glyphs at $4700, then OR the sword masks into six glyphs in each of the two rows.
Check the target's position against the drawn sword glyph range. On contact award points, then decrement the target's state or move it out of play and start the hit effect.
Select a two-row character patch on the other side of the player, save its old glyphs and compose the reflected sword by ORing in its second set of masks.
Compare the selected foreground object with the player using world-coordinate offsets. On overlap, remove vulnerable objects and apply damage once before starting a flash countdown and effect 4.
Translate the player's position into a screen cell and test the neighbouring glyph IDs. High glyph codes trigger health loss and a timed sprite flash.
When the companion's action is active, compare its world position with the selected target. Damage it or remove it and award decimal score if it is vulnerable.
Generate the $E000/$E100 object-record pointers in 12-byte steps from $C000. Generate the $E900/$BF00 glyph-address pairs in eight-byte steps from $4000.
Use the view origin to select source metatiles and expand their four character quadrants into the inactive screen matrix. Stage an additional expanded row at $0AB0–$0AFF to finish the scrolled view.
If the second object has not entered its action state, place it using the four area-specific position tables and select image 2.
Compare the second object's X and Y offsets against a 24-pixel window around the player. On overlap set its action and timing flags and request sound effect 7.
Select the stage-specific completion test. For the first four stages, discard the immediate caller's return and set the next disk selector in $FF when the test succeeds.

On the last stage's completion test, award a decimal score bonus and preserve the score for the high-score table. Use the raster handshake to switch video and print the stored ending one character at a time, then request the title.
Select the transition music, add a decimal score bonus and wait for the audio mode to signal the end before restoring the sprite-enable operand.
Reserve two drawing entries for player and companion. Scan object slots 2 through 30 for positions in the camera rectangle, then update the companion visibility flag separately.

Translate object X from world coordinates to view-relative coordinates. Expand its image descriptor into up to three sprite components, unpacking colour and mode bits and applying signed offsets to the later components.
Temporary byte holding the current component's packed attributes while $A4B8 through $A4D2 extract the bits.
Choose a candidate object from the visible list. Apply motion, derive a walking frame from its phase and facing bits, and turn on a blocking tile or missing support.
For object action 3, apply its movement and reverse its vertical direction when the terrain property differs from 8. Choose one of two images from its position.
For object action 4, read a timed direction sequence. Restart it at a negative marker and switch the object's image according to the action counter.
For object action 5, face the player and select the corresponding frame. A random threshold with the event idle arms an attack event and seeds object 20's position and state.
For object action 6, choose horizontal direction by comparing with the player. Use the vertical action counter to change climb or descent, then apply the combined motion.
When an area event is active, dispatch by stage and event number. Its first stage-one path times object 14's movement and clears the event and associated objects when the encounter ends.
Tick the area's movement timer, reverse object 14 at a terrain hit and choose its frame from the low position bit. Expiry changes its pose and restarts the event timer.
Use object 14's image index and position to choose a linked image and compute object 20's offset coordinates from five short tables.
Return byte between the linked-object routine and stage-two dispatch.
Route the current stage-two encounter by the event number in $11.
Use a timed direction sequence for object 13 and reposition it relative to the player at the third step. Copy its position to two linked objects and occasionally launch a projectile.
Route the three stage-five encounter numbers to their update routines.
Face the player with object 16, choose the accompanying draw frame and use the facing result to place a shot origin. Apply the random launch test.
Restore object 15 from its saved position and move it several times on a divided update using timed directions. Clear the event and hide its attached object after completion.
Project the scripted object's world position into a screen patch and copy eight rows of tile codes into whichever buffer the selector chooses. Set the attached object's image and offset position.

Set object 19 above the player on the area trigger, then update its direction using the player's relative X at the timer threshold. Copy its final position into object 20 or clear both when the area changes.
Cycle object 14 through six timed image and motion entries and move it twice per update. Clear the coordinates of objects left behind by the other event routines.
Move object 11 towards a nearby player when the terrain allows. Cycle its four images and restore its starting coordinates from one of two positions selected by its flag.
For the first event, tick its lifetime and move object 20. On each fourth action update select the next frame from a four-entry loop.
